title: Disclosure, human oversight, and misuse prevention

opening.headline: The extent to which AI use should be disclosed and whether important decisions can be left to AI are judged by dividing them into disclosure, human supervision, and prevention of misuse.
body: If part of the external presentation material was created with AI, should that fact be disclosed? If decisions that affect people's lives, such as hiring or taking out loans, are left to AI, who will be responsible? These questions do not require one answer, but different criteria depending on the situation.

In this lesson, we divide the problem into three prongs: disclosure, human oversight, and misuse prevention. Read how the three companies' usage policies address intent to deceive, and find out what human oversight means. After distinguishing that the principles document, safety framework, and usage policy answer different questions, we design disclosure and review as examples of public presentation materials.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can account for disclosure of AI use, human oversight, and prevention of misuse
Can distinguish between judgments that require human review
Determine whether protection and disclosure measures are appropriate

screens.title: How much will be revealed and who will make the final decision?
screens.lead: This is a scene where external presentation materials are being created. Read below and think about what questions this scene raises.

visual.alt: On the left is a mock-up of the external presentation slide, and on the right is a scene with a speech bubble indicating that this part was written by AI.

paragraphs: Let's say you drafted market analysis paragraphs and images for a presentation for an investor briefing using AI. Because of the urgent deadline, I wrote almost the first draft of the AI.

Three questions arise here. First, should we reveal that AI was used in this material? Second, who will ultimately verify and take responsibility for the figures and claims made by AI? Third, how do we prevent the same tool from being used to deceive others?
These three questions each address different topics: disclosure, human oversight, and misuse prevention. Today, we will divide these three and distinguish which documents answer which questions.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Is revealing that AI was used the same thing as having a human verify what AI wrote? By the end of the class, you will be able to distinguish between the two.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the three questions, let's first think about the situation that needed to be uncovered.

screens.title: A situation that had to be revealed
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever had a situation where you had to disclose that you used AI?
items.answer: These concerns often arise in posts that are published externally, such as official documents, investor materials, and notices to customers. At this time, the criteria are not the fact of use itself, but whether the reader misunderstands and the organization's disclosure rules.

items.prompt: What could have happened if you didn't disclose it?
items.answer: If the reader believes that the writing was written by a person and later finds out that the facts are different, trust may be shaken. In particular, intentionally misrepresenting a product as man-made may constitute a misuse prohibited by the policy.

items.prompt: Have you ever left important decisions to AI? Who made the final decision?
items.answer: If the structure is structured so that AI drafts and humans make decisions, responsibility is clear. Conversely, if the AI ​​outcome is decided immediately, there will be no one to take responsibility for when a problem arises. This difference can be summarized as human supervision.

screens.outro: Let's find the basis for disclosure in each company's policy.

screens.title: Disclosure of AI use and prevention of misuse
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare what the three companies' policies say about deception, impersonation, and high-risk automated decisions.

tabs.label: Google
tabs.body: Google's Generative AI Prohibited Use Policy classifies as misleading activity the misrepresentation of sources by claiming that content created with the intent to deceive was solely human-generated. This also applies to impersonating an individual without explicit disclosure with the intent to deceive. It also prohibits making automated decisions without human supervision that significantly disadvantage individual rights in high-risk areas such as employment, health care, finance, law, housing, insurance and social services.

tabs.label: Anthropic
tabs.body: Anthropic's Acceptable Use Policy prohibits misrepresenting the origin of content by impersonating any real person or entity or creating fake personas and accounts. This includes making you believe you are talking to a person. However, it is clearly stated that parodies, satire, and novels are not prohibited. In other words, the key is whether there is a purpose to deceive.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body: OpenAI's usage policy does not allow its services to be used to manipulate or deceive people, citing fraud, spam, and impersonation as examples. It also does not allow for automation of critical decisions in sensitive areas without human review.

tabs.label: Commonality and Monitoring
tabs.body: All three documents focus on intent to deceive and view misuse as unfairly avoiding disclosure. The service also has detection devices in place to prevent misuse. Gemini API states that abuses are first filtered out with an automated detection system, and projects with recurring suspicious activity are manually reviewed by authorized staff.

screens.outro: Now that we've distinguished between disclosure and misuse, let's see which judgments require human oversight.

screens.title: Judgments that require human supervision
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare what AI can do with what humans must do.

visual.alt: A picture with tasks that AI can do on the left, tasks to be decided by humans on the right, and an axis of difficulty in reversing in the middle.

states.label: What AI does
states.body: Organizing data, writing drafts, and comparing candidates are tasks that AI can best handle. The results can be read and corrected by humans, and it is easy to revert if mistakes are made. The Claude Constitution makes it a very important property that AI does not compromise human supervision, and supervision is not blind obedience. This means allowing someone with appropriate authority to stop or correct the AI. In a structure where such checks are possible, it is safe for AI to take over many tasks.

states.label: A person's decision
states.body: Decisions that have a large impact and are difficult to reverse are ultimately confirmed by humans. OpenAI states that humanity must control how AI is used and behaves, and Google's policies limit automated decisions without human supervision in high-risk areas such as employment, healthcare, finance, and law. This includes hiring decisions, loan approvals, and public announcement approvals. It should be structured so that a person makes the final decision, so that when a problem arises, it is clear who is responsible and there is still an opportunity for correction.

screens.outro: Now that we have seen the individual judgments, let us summarize that each document has a different role.

screens.title: What are the differences between principles, frameworks, and policies?
screens.lead: Each row of the table is a type of document, and the columns are what the document defines and targets. Compare row by row the reasons why the same company produces multiple documents.

data.caption: Purpose and target of each document type
rows: It describes how the model should behave and what values it should pursue.
Determine the model's direction of action. It is not a rule that users follow.
OpenAI Preparedness Framework, Google DeepMind Frontier Safety Framework, Anthropic Responsible Scaling Policy
We reveal the process by which developers check for dangerous capabilities, install safety measures, and then proceed with development and distribution.
This is the developer's internal procedure. These are not user rules.
OpenAI usage policies, Google's generative AI prohibition usage policy, Anthropic Usage Policy
It determines the permitted and prohibited uses for users.
These are the users and developers who use the service.
Our organization's security, disclosure, and review rules
We establish disclosure and review methods that members must follow when using AI in their work.
data.notes: OpenAI's Preparedness Framework tracks risky capabilities in the areas of biology and chemistry, cybersecurity, and self-improvement in AI. Google DeepMind's framework addresses how to set and check risky capability levels, while Anthropic's policy follows the principle of increasing safeguards proportional to risk.

screens.outro: Now that we've established that each document answers different questions, let's design disclosure and review in the case of a public presentation.

screens.title: Commentary: Design for disclosure and review of external presentation materials
screens.lead: The instructor explains step by step the process of designing disclosure and review in investor briefing materials. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: Some of the market analysis paragraphs and images in the investor briefing material were drafted with AI. Since this data becomes the basis for judgment by outsiders, both fact-checking and disclosure standards are required.

steps.title: Step 1: Separate and record the parts created by AI
steps.body: Displays and records which paragraphs and images were created by AI. Records are required to determine the scope of future review and serve as a basis for determining whether to disclose information.

steps.title: Step 2: Check the figures and citations in the original text
steps.body: Figures and quotes written by AI are compared with the original text. This is a human review. If incorrect numbers are communicated to investors, the impact is significant and difficult to reverse.

steps.title: Step 3: Mark according to your organization’s disclosure rules
steps.body: How to indicate the use of AI in documents released to the public depends on the organization's disclosure rules. The key is not to deceive the reader. It does not pretend to have been written by a person, but clearly states where the rules require it.

steps.title: Step 4: Determine the final approver
steps.body: Decide who will give final approval to the materials and that person will be responsible. If an approver is determined, AI errors can be prevented from being made public, and even when a problem arises, there is a clear path to correction.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: The ideal output is to have each section marked as Draft, Reviewed, Open, and Approved. The key to design is to include disclosure and review into the writing flow from the beginning rather than adding it at the end.

screens.outro: Now that you've seen how to incorporate disclosure and review into your design, let's determine how much is appropriate in each situation.

screens.title: Commentary: Are protection and disclosure measures appropriate?
screens.lead: Open each item one by one to determine what level of review and disclosure is appropriate in each of the three cases. It is useful to note how actions change as the risk increases.

items.title: Case A: Summary of internal meeting minutes
items.body: The results are only used within the organization and can be easily corrected if they are wrong. The risk is low, so a quick quick glance by the person who wrote the summary is sufficient. Open labeling is also not required unless organizational rules require it. However, we check before entering that it does not contain personal or confidential information.

items.title: Case B: Notice to customers
items.body: Since it is a text that is read and acted upon by outsiders, fact checking is required, and whether or not AI is used may need to be indicated in accordance with the organization's regulations. The figures, dates, and terms and conditions are verified by a human in the original text before being approved. Even if there is no intention to deceive, the standard is to ensure that readers do not misunderstand.

items.title: Case C: Hiring and lending decisions
items.body: It is a judgment that directly affects a person's life and is difficult to reverse. Human review and accountability are essential, and automated decisions without human oversight are subject to policy restrictions. AI must remain in an auxiliary role in organizing information, and decisions are made by humans. Here too, it is a good idea to take steps to check for bias.

items.title: Instructor's judgment
items.body: The greater the risk, the higher the level of review and disclosure. And it is easy to find evidence if you distinguish which document answers which question. The model's behavior is found in the principles document, the developer's risk management is found in the safety framework, and the usage rules I will follow are found in the usage policy and organizational regulations.

screens.outro: I will conclude the lesson with the conclusion that measures are proportional to risk.

screens.title: Bringing disclosure, oversight, and misuse prevention together
screens.lead: I will organize what I have seen so far into one judgment framework. Read it while thinking about the results you present to the outside world. It is helpful to determine at what stage each of the three prongs - disclosure, oversight, and misuse prevention - are needed.

paragraphs: Disclosure is intended to avoid deception. Misleading the reader by pretending it was man-made is considered misuse by all three companies' policies, and specific notation methods follow the organization's disclosure rules.

Human oversight is not about stopping AI from doing its work, but about allowing the right people to check and correct it. The bigger the impact and the more difficult it is to reverse the decision, the more important it is for someone to make the final confirmation and be responsible for it.

Each document has a different role. The principles document sets out the model's behavior, the safety framework sets out the developer's risk management procedures, and the usage policy sets out what users are allowed and prohibited to do. And on top of all of this are our organization's regulations. Knowing which documents answer which questions can help you quickly find evidence. On the other hand, if you read the documents with mixed roles, you may misunderstand the developer's internal procedures as rules you must follow.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Levels of review and disclosure are proportional to risk. The rules that users must follow are not in the safety framework, but in usage policies and organizational regulations.

glossary.def: It is about revealing that AI was used in content or judgment in accordance with the organization's rules and circumstances.
It is a device that allows humans to check the results and actions of AI and correct or stop it if necessary.
The policies and detection measures the Service has in place to prevent deception, impersonation, and dangerous use.
This is a process released by developers to measure dangerous capabilities, install safety measures, and then deploy them.
This is a document that sets out the permissible and prohibited rules that users must follow.

misconceptions.myth: The safety framework is the rules I have to follow.
misconceptions.fact: The safety framework is a document that reveals the developer's internal procedures. The rules to be followed by users are in the usage policy and organizational regulations.

misconceptions.myth: Anything created by AI must be labeled unconditionally.
misconceptions.fact: Whether and how it is written depends on the situation and organizational rules. The criterion is whether there is no purpose to deceive the reader.

misconceptions.myth: Human oversight is what prevents AI from doing its job.
misconceptions.fact: Oversight refers to ensuring that the appropriate people are able to inspect and correct AI. Even if AI takes on much of the work, oversight is maintained.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Disclosure is intended to be non-deceptive and follows the organization's rules.
Decisions with greater impact require human review and a responsible person.
Principle documents, safety frameworks and usage policies have different roles.
Levels of review and disclosure are proportional to risk.

checks.explain: Supervision is not about blind obedience, but about allowing inspection and correction. The larger the impact and the more difficult it is to reverse, the more likely it is that a human decision will be required.

wrong.1: Blind obedience is not the will of the bishop, the document explains.
wrong.2: The greater the risk, the higher the level of review, not the same level for all tasks.
